clue.text: The fault's in the office not the Church

definitions.text: The fault's in the office not the Church

parts.words: The fault's in the office not the Church
parts.note: a slip made by a desk worker, not by a member of the clergy, though the adjective could suggest either

explanation.surface: Someone insists the blame lies with the administrators, not the religious establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word of the answer can mean either office-related or priestly; the clue plays the two senses off each other.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake in copying or record-keeping is the standard phrase for an office slip-up.

clue.text: A fuel grid used as a protector

indicators.note: the letters are put to use in a fresh arrangement, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone repurposes part of a power network as a safety barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used' tells you to rearrange A FUEL GRID; 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A swimmer's guardian on a beach or at a pool protects bathers from drowning.

clue.text: First report on tree snake

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: the acer is the maple genus of tree

explanation.surface: Someone files the earliest sighting of a snake up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first letter of 'report' above ACER.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast-moving North American colubrid snake is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: Lively place for fast food

definitions.meaning: a chip shop, chiefly in Irish and northern English use

explanation.surface: A cheerful takeaway joint.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sprightly as an adjective and, as a noun, informally names a chip shop.

clue.text: Losing height, perhaps? Hardly!

indicators.note: signals that the letters may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Someone shrinking is asked if they are still tall and answers that they barely are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LOSING with H; the whole clue also describes the result: something that has lost height is only somewhat long.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has lost some height is now only fairly long, hardly long at all.

clue.text: A description of tennis to which I attach mainly commonsense

parts.note: real tennis is the old indoor form of the game
taken as written

indicators.note: most of the word, with its final letter removed

parts.note: to stick is to attach

explanation.surface: A tennis commentator adds some practical good sense to the description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mainly' drops the last letter of STICK to leave STIC; 'to which' is a link. Real tennis is the original indoor court game played in a few English and French venues.
explanation.definitionFit: Practical and sensible, grounded in what is achievable, matches the adjectival use of common sense.

clue.text: Ring followed by long think

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second in a down entry

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O
to pine is to long or yearn

explanation.surface: A phone call is followed by a long period of thought.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a view or reckon something is a synonym of expressing an opinion.

clue.text: Mixed, as in molecules

indicators.note: the letters are stirred together into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Something is jumbled up the way atoms combine in molecules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' rearranges AS IN MOLECULES, and the whole clue also describes the answer, since molecules are assortments of atoms.
explanation.definitionFit: Of various kinds, assorted and varied, is the meaning of this adjective.

clue.text: What the publican calls late on many occasions

definitions.text: What the publican calls late on many occasions

parts.words: What the publican calls late on many occasions
parts.note: a British pub landlord shouts the closing call repeatedly at the end of the night

explanation.surface: A landlord repeatedly calls out at closing time.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs the landlord calls 'Time!' at closing, often more than once; the phrase for 'repeatedly' is built from that call said again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means again and again, on many occasions, while picturing repeated closing calls.

clue.text: Disease? Iron is included in tonic for treatment

indicators.note: the element symbol is placed within the other letters
the letters are treated, worked over into a new order

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: An illness is treated with an iron-rich tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron is included in tonic' reads as a health drink, but 'in' gives its own letters: IN plus CTION (the rearranged TONIC, from 'for treatment'), with FE put inside the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A contracted illness caused by germs is a disease in the general sense.

clue.text: Politician in first-class cover-up

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written AI
Lib is short for a Liberal politician

explanation.surface: A top-flight politician is involved in a scandal hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-rate) is written with I for the figure 1.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse claiming one was elsewhere serves to cover up involvement in a crime.

clue.text: Calamitous reverses with no time for a smoke

indicators.note: having no time means going without it, so the letter for time is dropped from the reversed word
the word for calamitous is read backwards

parts.note: disastrous means tragic

explanation.surface: A disaster turns a smoker's leisure into no time for a cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverses' turns TRAGIC into CIGART, and 'with no' removes the T for time; 'for a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A rolled tobacco leaf is something one smokes, so a smoke can name one.

clue.text: Unexpected gripe about live changes producing special benefit

indicators.note: one set of letters goes around the other
the letters of gripe come out in an unexpected order
the letters of live are changed around

explanation.surface: A surprise complaint about altered living arrangements yields a perk.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIGE (from 'Unexpected' gripe) goes around VILE (from live 'changes'); 'about' looks like 'concerning' but is the container signal; 'producing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A right or advantage granted to a particular person or group is a special benefit.

clue.text: Field fire breaks out above the usual foliage

parts.note: a lea is a meadow or field

indicators.note: the letters of fire break free into a new order

explanation.surface: A grass fire erupts, overtaking the normal greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks out' gives FIER, and 'Field' is LEA, an old poetic word for a meadow; 'above the usual' turns the noun foliage into a comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative adjective means having more leaves, so more foliage than normal.

clue.text: Silicon confused with aluminium with the same slope

indicators.note: the letters are jumbled into another order

parts.note: Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium

explanation.surface: A chemist mixes up silicon and aluminium while measuring a gradient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges SILICON into ISOCLIN; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology and physics the term describes lines or strata of equal dip or inclination.

clue.text: Expression of admiration of hard and fast moves

indicators.note: the letters move around into a new order

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Applause for firm and swift movements.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'and' between the fodder words is a link; H for hard is the pencil-lead grading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exclamation of respect, from doffing a cap to someone admired.

clue.text: "The skull bone" — a class topic I put out

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, '"The skull bone" — a class topic I put out' (9): A CLASS TOPIC I has twelve letters against nine, with ASS left over and no clue word to remove it; no parse found and a quoted search gives nothing.
annotationWithheld.clue: "The skull bone" — a class topic I put out

clue.text: A right pair — useless and exhausting

parts.note: a duo is a pair
US stands for unserviceable, hence useless

explanation.surface: A tiring double act, both partners worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: US for unserviceable, meaning useless, is a crossword convention; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard work requiring great effort is tiring and exhausting in the same sense.

clue.text: Well up in singing — that's me

definitions.text: Well up in singing — that's me

parts.words: Well up in singing — that's me
parts.note: a singer whose voice is high up the scale describes their own place in a choir

explanation.surface: A singer boasts of being accomplished at their craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well up in' looks like 'skilled at', but it means high up the pitch range.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest female voice part sits well up the range in choral singing.

clue.text: Engineers get round to make the waste usable

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers of the British Army
to cycle is to go round in a circuit

explanation.surface: Army engineers set about reusing rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Processing used materials so they can be used again turns waste into something usable.

clue.text: Artist in East London, producer of a colourful display

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician
taken as written
Bow is a district of East London

explanation.surface: A painter in a London borough creates a bright show.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an area of the East End of London; RA marks a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc of spectral colours in the sky is the classic colourful display.

clue.text: European Union's typical split over trees

parts.note: EU is the abbreviation of European Union

indicators.note: the letters are split up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A European body is divided over forestry policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split' gives CALYPTI; 'over' is a link. The answer is the Latin plural, an accepted alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian gum trees take this Latin plural as an alternative to the regular form.

clue.text: Woodwork for a trunk?

parts.note: reads like carpentry for a chest, but means a small wood made up of tree trunks

explanation.surface: Someone asks about joinery for a storage chest.
explanation.walkthrough: Trunk suggests a box and woodwork suggests carpentry; both point instead to trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A small dense group of trees is a little wood, a thicket.

clue.text: Drank heavily back in the station

indicators.note: the word is read from back to front

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily

explanation.surface: Someone drinks hard on returning to the station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TOPED; 'in the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus or railway terminus, especially in American use, is a station.

clue.text: Sad song, for instance, to unburden heavenwards

indicators.note: in a down clue the letters are read upwards

parts.note: eg means for example
to rid is to free of a burden

explanation.surface: A mournful song offered skyward, to lift a weight from the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavenwards' reverses EGRID in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A lament for the dead is a mournful song.

clue.text: Separate and get a French drink in return

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: the word is read backwards

parts.note: a nip is a small drink

explanation.surface: A couple splits up and orders a French drink in exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' reverses NIP; 'and get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To detach by removing a fastening is to separate.

clue.text: Where one can't see the wood, they say!

definitions.text: Where one can't see the wood, they say!

parts.words: Where one can't see the wood, they say!
parts.note: alludes to the saying about not seeing the wood for the trees, applied to a place full of trees

explanation.surface: A remark about a place where it is hard to see the bigger picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'can't see the wood for the trees'; a tree collection fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A botanical garden devoted to trees is a place full of trees to look at.

clue.text: Trolley service?

parts.note: suggests a refreshment trolley, but means a service delivering food by vehicle

explanation.surface: A question about a refreshment cart.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain this is a service delivering hot food to the elderly or housebound.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a delivery of prepared food to people's homes by van.
